sections.b: Jubilees 17:15-18:19 retells Genesis 22 with a heavenly frame. Voices in heaven praise Abraham's faithfulness; Prince Mastema answers that Abraham loves Isaac more than anything and asks God to test him (17:16), as the accuser does in Job 1. The Lord already knows Abraham is faithful (17:17). At the altar the narrating angel stands beside Abraham, with Mastema watching, and the Lord sends him to stop the knife; Mastema "was put to shame" (18:12). The mountain is named as Mount Zion (18:13), and Abraham keeps a seven-day festival every year (18:18-19). The Qumran text 4Q225 (Pseudo-Jubilees) shares the frame of Mastemah's complaint.

common: Jubilees shifts the request for the test from God to Mastema, while keeping God in charge.
uncommon: Fitzmyer notes that the book's dates (17:15; 18:3) bring Abraham to the mountain on the fifteenth of the first month, Passover time, a link Jubilees makes "only indirectly".

sections.b: In Jubilees, Prince Mastema plays the accuser's part of Job 1-2. He challenges God to test Abraham (17:16) and is "put to shame" when Abraham obeys (18:12). Abraham promises that "the spirits of Mastema will not rule" over Jacob's line (19:28), since in this book evil spirits rule the nations but not Israel (15:31-32). The book uses the common noun säyṭan, "satan, adversary", separately: in the age of renewal there will be "no satan" (23:29).

sections.h: Ten trials and the friend of God (Jubilees)
sections.b: Jubilees lists the trials Abraham had already passed: his land, famine, the wealth of kings, his wife taken, circumcision, Ishmael and Hagar sent away (17:17). It numbers only the last: the burial of Sarah was "the tenth trial" (19:8), when he begged for a grave in the land promised to him and said nothing about the promise (19:3-9). The full count is Charles's: Ishmael and Hagar as two trials, the sixth and seventh, then Sarah's barrenness and the binding of Isaac (18) as the eighth and ninth. For that patience Abraham "was written down on the heavenly tablets as the friend of the Lord" (19:9), the title of 2 Chronicles 20:7 and James 2:23. The Mishnah also speaks of ten trials (Mishnah Avot 5:3).

Jubilees fills the years Genesis leaves empty. Abraham gives three farewell speeches: to all his descendants (20), to Isaac, with the priestly laws of sacrifice (21), and to Jacob, whom he blesses as heir (22). He keeps a last Feast of Weeks with Isaac and Ishmael (22:1-9) and dies in the night with Jacob asleep in his arms (22:26-23:3). Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah (23:7; Genesis 25:9).

Jubilees clears Ishmael of blame: he is only "playing and dancing" when Sarah grows jealous (17:4). He comes to Abraham's last Feast of Weeks and mourns with Isaac at his death (22:1-3; 23:6-7). His sons and Keturah's settle from Paran to the entrance of Babylon and are called "Arabs and Ishmaelites" (20:12-13).

sections.b: Jubilees retells Hagar's sending away (17:8-12) and adds that she died before Sarah, which is why Abraham did not take her back but married Keturah, "one of the children of the servants born in his household" (19:11). Charles notes that later rabbinic tradition took the opposite path and identified Keturah with Hagar.

Jubilees has Abraham love Jacob, as Rebekah does, while Isaac loves Esau (19:15, 31). Jacob learns to write; Esau learns war (19:14). Abraham charges Rebekah to guard Jacob (19:16-25), blesses him with the blessings of Adam, Enoch, Noah and Shem (19:27-29; 22:10-30), gives him his house (22:24) and dies with him in his arms (23:1-3). Genesis never brings the two together.

sections.h: Jubilees 23: shrinking lives and their return
sections.b: Jubilees 23:9-31 turns the shrinking life spans of Genesis into a vision. The ancients lived nineteen jubilees; after the Flood lives shortened, and even Abraham did not reach four jubilees. An evil generation will grow old before two jubilees, gray-haired as children (23:11, 25), and seventy or eighty will count as long (23:12, 15; Psalm 90:10). When the children return to the law, lives will lengthen toward a thousand years and there will be no old men (23:26-28), as Isaiah 65:20 promises.

sections.h: Jubilees 23:31: bones at rest, spirits in joy
sections.b: "Their bones will rest in the earth, and their spirits will have much joy" (Jubilees 23:31). R. H. Charles read this as no resurrection of the body but a blessed life of the spirit after death, like 1 Enoch 91-104, and called it the earliest attested instance of that hope in the last two centuries BC. He weighed whether "they will rise up" (23:30) means a raising of the dead and judged that it apparently means rising in health. The verse itself says only that the bodies of the righteous rest while their spirits rejoice.

sections.h: Jubilees 23: the evil generation and the return to the law
sections.b: Jubilees 23:16-31 pictures an evil generation: sons accuse their fathers of forsaking the covenant and the calendar, there is strife between young and old and rich and poor, blood is shed, the holy place is defiled, and merciless nations invade. Then the children begin to study the law, lives lengthen, and there is no satan. Charles read it as a veiled history of the Maccabean age; it also belongs with the woes of Matthew 24 and the visions of 4 Ezra.

Abraham forbids Isaac to eat blood (21:6, 18), tells him to cover spilled blood with dirt (21:17; Leviticus 17:13), and to take no payment for a human life: "Blood for blood" (21:19-20; Numbers 35:31-33). The earth cannot be cleansed of human blood except by the blood of the killer.

Jubilees 21:7-16 has Abraham teach Isaac the peace offering and its fat (Leviticus 3), the two-day limit for eating it (Leviticus 19:6), salt on every offering ("the covenant of salt", Numbers 18:19), a list of woods fit for the altar, and washing before and after offering (Exodus 30:19-21). The book claims these rules came down in the books of Enoch and Noah (21:10). The Testament of Levi 9 hands the same rules from Isaac to Levi.

Abraham's charge to Jacob is the strongest call in Jubilees to keep apart from Gentiles: do not eat with them, do not copy their deeds, do not marry the daughters of Canaan, for they sacrifice to the dead and bow to demons (22:16-22; compare 20:4). R. H. Charles saw the pressure of Antiochus IV behind it. The same issue of table fellowship returns in Acts 10:28 and Galatians 2:11-14.

In the year he dies, Isaac and Ishmael come to keep "the Feast of Weeks, which is the feast of the first fruits of the harvest" with Abraham (22:1). Isaac offers sacrifices, Rebekah sends cakes of the new grain, and Abraham thanks God and blesses Jacob (22:4-30). The covenant feast thus becomes the setting for passing the blessing to Jacob.

Abraham, who burned the idol house in his youth, warns all his sons: idols are empty, have no spirit and are the work of hands (20:7-8). He tells Isaac that his soul has hated idols (21:3) and mocks those who say to wood "You are my God" and to a stone "You are my Lord" (22:18; Jeremiah 2:27).

sections.h: The mountain of the binding is Zion (Jubilees 18)
sections.b: Jubilees names the mountain where Isaac was bound: "It is Mount Zion" (18:13). Genesis says only "the land of Moriah"; 2 Chronicles 3:1 puts Solomon's Temple "on Mount Moriah". Jubilees joins the binding and the Temple mount explicitly.

Jubilees calls Machpelah "the double cave", as the Septuagint does. Abraham buys it for Sarah (19:5-6), and Isaac and Ishmael bury him there beside her (23:7). The Ge'ez gives the price as forty pieces of silver; the Latin and Genesis have four hundred.
